messages:
Kelly (ACME SecOps): Hey team — our private deploy in us-east-1 started failing KMS unwraps around 12:30 UTC. App logs show `KMS: tls handshake failed: alert 40` and upstream /decrypt calls time out (504). This is only on the VPC deployment behind NATGW. Any pointers?
Maria (Support): Thanks Kelly — can you paste the KMS endpoint you hit and a small log snippet? Also does this fail from all app nodes or only some?
Kelly (ACME SecOps): Endpoint is `https://kms.private.acme.acme-internal:8443`. Fails from 3/5 app nodes intermittently. Log snippet: `2026-03-17T12:31:02Z ERROR kmsclient: handshake failed: tls: received alert handshake failure (alert 40)`
Ajay (Oncall): Intermittent handshake failures in private networks often point at SNI/misconfigured client certs, or an egress device (proxy/NAT) mangling TLS. Can you run these from a failing node and paste outputs?
  1) `dig +short kms.private.acme.acme-internal`
  2) `curl -v --resolve 'kms.private.acme.acme-internal:8443:10.0.5.12' https://kms.private.acme.acme-internal:8443/health`
  3) `openssl s_client -connect 10.0.5.12:8443 -servername kms.private.acme.acme-internal -brief`
Kelly (ACME SecOps): Ran them — dig -> `10.0.5.12`. curl output: `* Connected to kms.private.acme.acme-internal (10.0.5.12) port 8443 (#0)
* TLS handshake error`
OpenSSL minimal: `CONNECTED(00000003)
140437233421376:error:14094410:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:tlsv1 alert handshake failure:ssl/record/rec_layer_s3.c:1543:SSL alert number 40`
Maria (Support): Good info. Two immediate checks: (A) confirm the client is sending the expected SNI (openssl test does that with `-servername`), and (B) confirm the HSM/KMS expects a client cert or specific TLS version. Also check whether there's an HTTP/TCP proxy or L7 device between app and 10.0.5.12 that could rewrite SNI or terminate TLS.
Kelly (ACME SecOps): We're NATing via TGW + NATGW. Vendor says they sometimes see connections from unexpected source IPs and reject them if client cert missing. How can we prove the SNI/client cert are present from the app side?
Ajay (Oncall): For SNI: `openssl s_client -connect 10.0.5.12:8443 -servername kms.private.acme.acme-internal -msg` will show ClientHello with SNI. For client certs, use `-cert /path/to/cert.pem -key /path/to/key.pem` and watch the handshake. If the vendor sees mismatched source IP you might be hitting SNAT on the NATGW — confirm the HSM allowlist contains the NATGW EIP(s).
DevEx-Mike: Also don't forget path MTU/fragmentation issues can cause intermittent TLS handshake failures if the handshake contains large extensions (client certs). Try lowering MSS or enable MSS clamping on the NATGW/CFW. Quick check: `sudo iptables -t mangle -A POSTROUTING -p tcp --sport 443 -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu` (test only) or run `tracepath 10.0.5.12` to see MTU drop.
Kelly (ACME SecOps): We ran openssl with `-servername` and it still fails. Vendor said they see some connects with no SNI and some with SNI, weird. Could an internal proxy remove SNI?
Maria (Support): Yes — some L7 proxies or TLS-terminating appliances can strip or rewrite SNI if they're doing TLS passthrough incorrectly. Check sidecars (istio/envoy) or any transparent proxies on the path. For testing: from an app node `tcpdump -n -s0 -w /tmp/kms.pcap host 10.0.5.12 and port 8443` while you run openssl; then we can inspect the ClientHello SNI field with `tshark -r /tmp/kms.pcap -Y 'ssl.handshake.extensions_server_name' -V` (or `-T fields -e ssl.handshake.extensions_server_name`).
Ajay (Oncall): Also validate DNS resolution across nodes — inconsistent DNS (split-horizon) can cause some nodes to resolve to a different backend IP that expects different TLS config. Compare `getent hosts kms.private.acme.acme-internal` output across good/bad nodes.
Kelly (ACME SecOps): Quick outputs: good node getent -> `10.0.5.12`, bad node getent -> `10.0.5.13`. Vendor says .12 expects client cert, .13 expects token-based auth. That would explain intermittent behavior. How do we ensure consistent DNS?
Maria (Support): Sounds like split-horizon or stale DNS cache on some nodes. Check your node-local DNS cache (systemd-resolved/nscd/kube-dns). For k8s, check CoreDNS pods: `kubectl -n kube-system logs coredns-xxxx`. If you use node-local cache, restart the caching process on the bad nodes to force refresh. Also check any Route53 private hosted zone TTLs and whether both ENIs are registered.
Kelly (ACME SecOps): We do use CoreDNS with node-local proxies. We'll restart CoreDNS on the two bad nodes and rerun tests.
sre-bot: deploy-bot: Canary rollback triggered for `private-kms-route` at 12:40 UTC — this might have changed backend IP mapping.
Maria (Support): Ah — that rollback could be the root cause: backend mapping changed while some nodes still had cached DNS pointing to old backends. Steps to resolution we recommend: 
  1) Restart node DNS cache / CoreDNS to flush stale records.
  2) Confirm HSM/KMS allowlist includes NATGW EIPs (or avoid SNAT so source IPs match vendor expectations).
  3) Capture a pcap from a failing node and confirm whether ClientHello SNI present: `tcpdump -n -s0 -w /tmp/kms.pcap host 10.0.5.12 and port 8443` then inspect with tshark.
  4) If vendor requires client certs, test with `openssl s_client -connect 10.0.5.12:8443 -cert client.pem -key client.key -servername kms.private.acme.acme-internal` to confirm successful handshake.
  5) Check MTU/MSS clamping if certificate chains are large and handshake packets get fragmented.
Kelly (ACME SecOps): Great checklist — restarting CoreDNS on the two nodes fixed consistent resolution to .12 and after a test with `openssl -cert` the handshake succeeds. We'll coordinate with the vendor to add NATGW EIPs to their allowlist and investigate avoiding SNAT for these flows. Thanks everyone :thumbsup:
Maria (Support): Glad that helped — marking this thread for follow-up: ask vendor to confirm allowlist update and let us know if you want us to review a pcap. If you hit the issue again, ping and attach `/tmp/kms.pcap`.
Kelly (ACME SecOps): Will do, thanks!
